media.description: This man seems to be pleading with the Gods above. That's Romulus, the legendary founder of Rome. He has thrown this lavish banquet and is trying to convince the Gods to admit the many rulers of Rome, who are assembling down below. A crucial invite for these glory-seeking emperors. The Gods rather mischievously suggest that a competition takes place, and only the winners should be allowed to attend….

Each emperor jostles for a seat at this table. Julius Caesar has forced himself to the front of course, centre-stage, confident that he will be one of the chosen few. I think as Verrio painted this, he may have been inspired by some of the pompous courtiers he witnessed here at Hampton court!

And that's Nero to the right, strumming away on his guitar. He's trying to flatter the gods by modelling himself on Apollo, but Apollo wasn't at all impressed… I will soon take off that wreath. For he does not imitate me in all things, and even when he does he does it badly. He's swiftly rejected by the Gods. How unfortunate for him!

On his Donkey is Silenus, court jester to the Gods. He humbles the emperors, taunting them with his jibes. ake care Zeus, lest this man in his lust for power rob you of your empire. His insults help the Gods decide who might be allowed into the feast and many are swiftly dismissed. Good heavens! What a changeable monster is this! What mischief will [Octavian] do us?
These little floating creatures are Furies, Goddesses of vengeance and justice. They punish those Emperors deemed unworthy.

Here we have a figure, a little more separate from the rest of the group that the artist Verrio has paid plenty of attention to. Such prowess, such glory. This is the Macedonian emperor, Alexander the Great, who has arrived into the scene as the guest of his promoter Herakles, a hero from Greek mythology … Alexander ruled over an empire even larger, we're told, than the Roman emperors. We can see the Winged figure of Victory swooping in to place a laurel wreath upon his head, in celebration of his victories. See now whether all these Romans can match this one Greek.

Back to today - William III does like to see himself as Herakles and Alexander. Herakles was famous for his super-human strength and Alexander for his military conquests – great attributes for a warrior king like William. But also, just like Alexander amidst all these Romans, William is a bit of an outsider. He is Dutch, but swept to power here in England with his English wife Queen Mary II during the Glorious Revolution of 1688. A spectacular painting like this might just be enough to convince some of our important guests here at Hampton Court of William and Mary's entitlement to the crown. That they too deserve a seat at the table of the gods.

Talking of Queen Mary … sitting peacefully on her crescent, is Diana, Goddess of the moon. Just as we're meant to think of William as Alexander the Great, then perhaps Verrio has painted Mary as Diana. Our tragic queen who died of smallpox in 1694. Before we leave the Staircase, and enter the royal apartments, turn to the north wall …

The bountiful harvest scene represents the abundance and prosperity that comes from divine favor. These agricultural symbols remind us of the earthly realm and the connection between divine blessing and human prosperity.

These playful cherubs represent the innocent and pure aspects of the divine realm. Their presence brings joy and lightness to the scene, symbolizing the happiness that comes from divine favor and protection.

The celestial musicians provide the soundtrack to this divine assembly. Their harmonious melodies accompany the proceedings, creating an atmosphere of celebration and divine grandeur that befits such an important gathering.

The artist's signature marks the completion of this magnificent work. Verrio's name immortalized in this grand staircase, a testament to the skill and vision that brought this divine scene to life for all to marvel at.
